reading.title: Part 1: Reading - The Evolution of Cloud Computing
reading.reading_passage:
A decade ago, most companies hosted their digital infrastructure on physical servers located in their own office buildings. This approach, known as 'on-premises' hosting, required massive upfront investments in hardware and dedicated IT staff to maintain the machines. Today, however, the corporate landscape has been transformed by cloud computing. By utilizing cloud providers like Amazon Web Services (AWS) or Microsoft Azure, businesses can rent computing power and storage space over the internet on a pay-as-you-go basis.

The primary advantage of cloud computing is its unparalleled scalability. If an e-commerce website experiences a sudden surge in traffic during a holiday sale, the cloud infrastructure can automatically allocate more resources to keep the site running smoothly. Once the sale ends, the resources scale back down, ensuring the company only pays for what it uses. Furthermore, cloud computing facilitates remote work by allowing employees to access company data and applications from anywhere in the world. Despite concerns regarding data sovereignty and reliance on third-party vendors, the flexibility and cost-efficiency of the cloud make it an indispensable tool for modern enterprises.

reading.title: Part 2: Reading - AI in Cybersecurity
reading.reading_passage:
As cyber threats become increasingly sophisticated, human security analysts are struggling to keep pace. Hackers are now using automated scripts to launch thousands of attacks simultaneously, probing networks for vulnerabilities. In response, cybersecurity firms are turning to Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) to bolster their defenses. Unlike traditional antivirus software, which relies on known signatures of malicious files, AI systems are designed to recognize abnormal behavior.

For example, if an employee's account suddenly begins downloading gigabytes of sensitive data at 3:00 AM from an unrecognized IP address, the AI system will immediately flag this as anomalous behavior and lock the account. This proactive approach allows organizations to stop data breaches before they inflict severe damage. However, AI is a double-edged sword. Cybercriminals are also leveraging machine learning to craft highly convincing phishing emails and to develop malware that can adapt its code to evade detection. Therefore, the future of digital security will likely be a perpetual arms race between defensive AI and offensive AI.

reading.title: Part 3: Reading - Agile Methodology in Software Engineering
reading.reading_passage:
In the early days of software engineering, teams predominantly used the 'Waterfall' methodology. This linear approach required developers to complete one phase of a project entirely—such as design, coding, or testing—before moving on to the next. While structured, Waterfall was rigid; if a client requested a fundamental change late in the development cycle, it often led to disastrous delays and budget overruns.

To address these flaws, the tech industry widely adopted 'Agile' methodology. Agile breaks projects down into smaller, manageable iterations known as 'sprints', typically lasting two to four weeks. At the end of each sprint, the team delivers a functional piece of the software to the client for immediate feedback. This iterative process allows developers to pivot quickly if the project's requirements change. Furthermore, Agile promotes daily communication within cross-functional teams, breaking down silos between developers, testers, and operations. Ultimately, while Agile demands a high degree of collaboration and adaptability, it results in software that better aligns with the end-user's actual needs.
